newsitem.title: FRANCE: French trucker talks inch forward, protests go on.
newsitem.headline: French trucker talks inch forward, protests go on.

text.p: Striking truck drivers tightened their stranglehold on French highways and fuel supplies with 176 roadblocks on Tuesday, after a fifth round of talks with employers broke off with little progress on key demands.
Union officials said the popular nine-day-old protest for wage hikes, shorter working hours and early retirement was growing in strength and putting greater pressure on the economy.
The south and west of the country were worst affected. But truckers also sealed off a petrol depot at Grigny which supplies 90 percent of petrol sold in hypermarkets in the Paris region.
The Oil Industry Association said half the nation's 175 fuel depots were blocked. Heating fuel was getting through, but 500 out of 18,000 petrol stations ran dry, up from 100 on Monday.
Local authorities ordered a growing number of petrol stations around the country to only supply firemen and ambulances, or rationed sales to motorists to half a tank.

The strike started affecting mail distribution and disrupting grain supplies to French ports. A spokesman for the Fleury Michon food company said 70 to 80 percent of food supplies had gone through so far, but the food industry would suffer major losses if the strike went on for a couple of days.
The national traffic information centre reported trucks parked across 176 main roads across France at 11 a.m. (1000 GMT), either blocking or snarling traffic.

Marathon talks suspended at 6.30 a.m. (0530 GMT) were due to resume at 3 p.m. (1400 GMT). Government mediator Robert Cros reported "significant progress" with agreement in principle on changes in sick leave, travel expenses and a ban on trucks of all nationalities from French roads on Sundays.

Employers' spokesman Jehan de Marne said the atmosphere at the talks was serene and positive, but both sides needed time to study technical issues, including the truckers' demand to bring retirement forward to 55 from 60.

Unions said progress was insufficient to justify loosening the screw. The Force Ouvriere (FO) union said employers would not budge on wage demands, including paying for the time truckers waste waiting to load and unload.
"It is in the truckers' interest to exert maximum pressure to make employers understand that they will gain nothing by digging in their heels," said CGT leader Louis Viannet.

The French franc fell on the news that talks had stalled. Traders said fears the strike could spread or the government could agree to the strikers' demands weighed on the currency, pushing it below 3.39 to the German mark.
Government spokesman Alain Lamassoure said the government was ready to help meet some of the drivers' key demands by facilitating early retirement and reducing payroll taxes.

He asked other unions to reconsider threats to jump on the truckers' bandwagon and stage their own strikes. "It certainly isn't in the interest of road haulage employees, because some of their demands are legitimate," he told RTL radio.
FO leader Marc Blondel has threatened to extend the strike to rail and air transport unless a deal is reached by Tuesday.

The CGT has called for nationwide demonstrations and rallies at the roadblocks on Wednesday. Five rail unions urged members to support the truckers "with the appropriate means". The CFDT said widening the strike would defuse the truckers' protest.

Trade unions have announced plans for a 24-hour strike at state-owned utilities Electricite de France and Gaz de France on December 3, and for a two-day crew strike at Air France and other French airlines on Wednesday and Thursday.
Among new roads targetted by blockades on Tuesday were the A31 motorway between Nancy and the Luxembourg border, the A4 motorway east of Reims, and the Pont de Normandie.

In Normandy, all petrol depots and refineries near Rouen, including Royal Dutch Shell and Total, were sealed off. British truckers arriving at the Channel port of Calais were virtual prisoners in the ferry terminals.
